title: Influences of culture and environmental attitude on thermal, emotional and perceptual evaluations of a public square
research_question: To examine the influence of culture (Swedish vs Japanese) and environmental attitude (urban vs open-air person) on participants' thermal, emotional and perceptual assessments of a public square, within the PET comfortable interval of 18-23°C.

participants.description: 43 Swedish and 63 Japanese participants, 55% Swedish women, 40% Japanese women. Age ranges: 15-80 years. Participants self-identified as urban vs open-air persons and visited squares within PET 18-23°C.
participants.recruitment: Participants were selected because they estimated themselves as urban vs open-air persons and happened to visit the square within the PET thermal comfortable interval of 18-23°C.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Swedish square: Gustav Adolfs torg, Göteborg (57°42′N, 11°58′E). Traditional European square, approx. 100x60m, cobblestones, buildings, canal, row of trees (little shade, strong wind exposure).

Japanese square: Matsudo Station Square, Matsudo (35°78N, 139°90E). Modern functional square, in front of railway station, lifted one level, approx. 50x40m, light clinkers, 0.4m wall, no trees (little shade).

measures.construct: Perceived current weather (good/bad for outdoor activity)

measures.instrument: RayMan model (calculated from air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, short-wave radiation, long-wave radiation)

mechanisms: Thermal, emotional and perceptual assessments of a physical place may be intertwined with psychological schema-based and socio-cultural processes.
Cultural response bias (e.g., modesty in Japan) may influence self-reported evaluations.
Architectural design differences between the squares may contribute to cultural differences in perceptual evaluation.
A person's mood may influence their evaluation of the aesthetics of a physical place.
implementation_implications: Thermal comfort indices may not be applicable in different cultural/climate zones without modifications.
Thermal comfort indices may not be appropriate if psychological processes involved in environmental assessment are not taken into account.

tables.description: Influence of cold/warm perception of current weather (independent variable) on thermally comfortable.
Influence of glad/gloomy on the site (independent variable) on beautiful/ugly and pleasant/unpleasant.

limitations: Participants were not randomly assigned to groups, leading to potential confounding with uncontrolled extraneous variables and weaker causal inferences.
Potential 'cultural response bias' in Japanese participants, who might have evaluated the square and their feelings more modestly due to cultural values.
Differences in architectural design between the Swedish and Japanese squares might have contributed to the observed cultural differences in perceptual evaluation.
